\chapter{Communication Complexity — Indexing: Basic}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.CommunicationComplexity.DeterministicCC.FuncIndexing.Basic
\section{Overview}

This module introduces the Index problem $\mathrm{IND}_n$: Alice holds an $n$-bit string
$x : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathrm{Bool}$, Bob holds an index $i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,n$, and the
answer is the bit $x_i$.  It defines the function and the trivial one-way protocol, shows
that the deterministic one-way communication complexity of $\mathrm{IND}_n$ is exactly $n$
and that the two-way deterministic complexity is at most $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 1$, and
packages the uniform distribution on input pairs $(x, i)$ used by the distributional lower
bound in the companion module.  Throughout, $n$ is a positive natural number.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[The Index function]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing}
\leanok
The Index function on $n$ bits: given Alice's string $x : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathrm{Bool}$
and Bob's index $i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,n$, it returns Alice's $i$-th bit,
$\mathrm{indexing}_n(x, i) := x_i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Trivial one-way protocol for Index]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.trivialProtocol}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.trivialProtocol}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol}
The one-way protocol for Index in which Alice sends her entire string $x$ as the message
(the message type is $\mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathrm{Bool}$ and the send map is the identity),
and Bob outputs the $i$-th bit of the received message.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[One-way complexity of Index is at most $n$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.oneWayCommunicationComplexity_le}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.oneWayCommunicationComplexity_le}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.cost, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.communicationComplexity_le_iff, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.trivialProtocol}
The deterministic one-way communication complexity of $\mathrm{IND}_n$ is at most $n$:
\[
  D^{\to}(\mathrm{IND}_n) \le n,
\]
as witnessed by the trivial protocol in which Alice sends all $n$ bits of her string.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Two-way complexity of Index is at most $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 1$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.communicationComplexity_le}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.communicationComplexity_le}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity_le_clog_card_Y_alpha, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing}
The (two-way) deterministic communication complexity of $\mathrm{IND}_n$ is at most
$\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 1$:
\[
  D(\mathrm{IND}_n) \le \lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 1,
\]
where $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ is formalised as $\mathrm{Nat.clog}\,2\,n$.  This is the
protocol in which Bob sends his index $i$ and Alice replies with the single bit $x_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[One-way complexity of Index is at least $n$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.le_oneWayCommunicationComplexity}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.le_oneWayCommunicationComplexity}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.Computes, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.cost, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.le_communicationComplexity_iff, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing}
Every correct deterministic one-way protocol for $\mathrm{IND}_n$ has cost at least $n$;
that is,
\[
  n \le D^{\to}(\mathrm{IND}_n).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exact one-way complexity of Index]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.oneWayCommunicationComplexity_eq}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.oneWayCommunicationComplexity_eq}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.le_oneWayCommunicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.oneWayCommunicationComplexity_le}
The deterministic one-way communication complexity of $\mathrm{IND}_n$ is exactly $n$:
\[
  D^{\to}(\mathrm{IND}_n) = n.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Uniform input distribution for Index]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexingInputDist}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexingInputDist}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace.of}
The hard input distribution for Index: the uniform probability measure on pairs $(x, i)$
in $\mathrm{BoolInput}\,n \times \mathrm{Fin}\,n$, so that Alice's string $x$ and Bob's
index $i$ are chosen independently and uniformly at random.  It is packaged as a
finite probability space whose measure is $\mathrm{uniformOn}\,\mathrm{Set.univ}$.
\end{definition}
